title: The bird on the 11,000 V line
hook: Birds perch on bare power lines every day. What voltage is across one?

doesNotKnow: that voltage is a difference between two points
that current flows through something only when its two ends sit at different voltages

misconception: A bird on an 11,000 V line has 11,000 V through it and survives only because birds are insulated or lucky.
objective: The learner can explain that voltage is a difference between two points: a bird on one line has almost no voltage between its feet, so almost no current flows through it, but touching the grounded pole puts the full 11,000 V across it.

claims.text: Current through a conductor needs a potential difference across it (I = ΔV / R); reveal: 'Current needs a voltage difference to push it, so almost none goes through the bird.'
claims.source: Ohm's law: any introductory electricity text (e.g. OpenStax University Physics Vol. 2, chapter 9, Current and Resistance; fact-checker picks the section). Brief: company/domains/briefs/physics.electricity.md round 3 #2, claim 1.

claims.text: On a line at 11,000 V to ground carrying 200 A, each foot reads 11,000 V against ground, and the wire between feet 5 cm apart drops 0.002 V (2 cm: 0.001 V; 20 cm: 0.008 V); stage: 'feet 11,000 V', 'across 5 cm 0.002 V'; reveal: 'only 0.002 V between them'.
claims.source: ΔV = I R' L with I = 200 A, R' = 0.2 ohm/km: 200 x 0.0002 x 0.05 = 0.002 V (Demo.tsx `acrossV`, shown with toFixed(3); 7 cm gives 0.0028 -> '0.003 V'). Foot 2 reads 11,000 - 0.002 V, shown rounded as 11,000 V. Current and conductor resistance are illustrative (brief claim 2; check.mjs); real line currents and conductors vary.

claims.text: With feet on one line, the current through the bird is about 0.2 µA (stage: 'bird 0.2 µA'); with a wing on the grounded pole, 11,000 V is across it and about 1.1 A flows (stage: 'bird 1.1 A', 'to pole 11,000 V'; reveal: 'the difference jumped to 11,000 V').
claims.source: I = ΔV / R with an illustrative bird resistance of 10 kilo-ohm (brief): 0.002 / 10,000 = 2e-7 A; 11,000 / 10,000 = 1.1 A. Arrow width grows with log10 of the current (Demo.tsx comment), so it is a picture of order of magnitude, not a linear scale. Electrocution of birds that bridge a conductor and a grounded pole or two conductors is documented in APLIC, Suggested Practices for Avian Protection on Power Lines (2006) (fact-checker confirms).

claims.text: The pole is drawn as grounded (0 V), with the line held off it by an insulator.
claims.source: Distribution poles carry grounded hardware (ground wires, bonded crossarm fittings) and the conductor sits on insulators; APLIC (2006) describes grounded hardware as the electrocution path for perching birds. Stage drawing only (no stage text). Fact-checker confirms the wording.

claims.text: Never approach real power lines: current can jump across air.
claims.source: High voltages can arc across an air gap: the breakdown field of dry air is about 3 MV/m (any electrostatics text, e.g. OpenStax University Physics Vol. 2, section 7.5); utility safety guidance keeps people metres from lines. SAFETY WORDING: must be approved by a reader other than its author before publish (W-361 precedent; brief).

claims.text: Model: the line is drawn at a steady 11,000 V; on an AC line both feet rise and fall together, so the difference between them stays tiny.
claims.source: Brief claim 5. On AC the line-to-ground voltage varies in time, but both feet sit on the same conductor a few cm apart, so their difference is still I(t) R' L, thousandths of a volt. Stated here and in the Demo.tsx header; not on the stage (text budget).

recall.question: A squirrel sitting on one power line reaches over and touches a second line at a different voltage. Why is that dangerous when sitting on one line was not?
options: Now there is a voltage difference between the two points it touches
Two lines carry twice the current into it
It is no longer insulated by its feet
recall.why: Current flows through something only when its two ends are at different voltages. On one line both feet are at almost the same voltage; two different lines put a large difference across the animal.
